groups.text: Every time a J V M starts, it redoes the same work.
The first time code touches a class, the J V M loads it, links it, and resolves its references.
The first call of a lambda does more.
Its invokedynamic instruction runs a bootstrap method that generates the lambda's class.
On J D K twenty-five, one start of a three hundred-class app took four hundred thirty-one ms of wall time, and the next start pays it all again.
Project Leyden moves that work out of production runs.
Its first result is the A O T cache, which you build in three phases.
First, a training run.
You run the app with a representative workload.
The J V M records what the app loaded and linked into an A O T configuration file, and on J D K twenty-five also its method profiles.
Second, assembly. The J V M turns that file into the cache.
Your application does not run.
Third, production. Every start after that names the cache.
On J D K twenty-five, one command with AOTCacheOutput does the first two phases.
It trains, then starts a second J V M to assemble the cache.
The cache stores the results of start-up work from the training run.
Classes already loaded and linked.
Symbolic references already resolved to the real method.
Lambda call sites already resolved.
Objects the J V M would build at start-up, such as its module graph.
And on J D K twenty-five, the method profiles that tell the jit what is hot.
In production, the J V M loads and links every cached class before main even starts.
Then main runs without stopping for them.
For the three hundred-class app, wall time fell from four hundred thirty-one ms to ninety-eight.
C P U time fell from five hundred four ms to eighty-one, and peak memory from sixty-four to forty-two MiB.
Code the training run never touched gets none of this.
It is resolved lazily, as before.
So train with a workload that looks like production.
